title: Teaching on Purpose 6
author: Kohlbeck, Adam
summary: The sixth instalment in Adam Kohlbeck's Teaching on Purpose series (Chiltern Learning Trust), this article focuses on the purpose of 'Communicating Meaning' through the I Do, We Do, You Do instructional model, illustrated by an interview with Henry Cross, Assistant Headteacher at Challney High School for Boys. The article traces the pedagogical logic of gradual release: the teacher models explicitly with live narration during 'I do,' shifts to collaborative co-construction during 'We do' where mini-whiteboards and whole-class circulation allow responsive checking and adjustment, and then releases students to independent application during 'You do.' The author distinguishes when this model should be used as described (new concept, new task, new skill), when teachers might compress or skip the 'We do' (secure prior knowledge), and crucially when they should use alternative sequences (e.g., 'You do, then I do' for generating prior knowledge before instruction). The piece illustrates a key tension in instructional design: the default 'I do, We do, You do' sequence is not universal but appropriate when students genuinely need a model before attempting; using it when students already have the schema wastes instructional time and underestimates learner readiness.
points: Gradual release (I do, We do, You do) works because it stages the transfer of cognitive load from teacher to student incrementally -- but the critical decision is diagnosing whether students actually need that scaffold before attempting the task.

The 'We do' phase is the most nuanced: mini-whiteboards and visible simultaneous responses allow the teacher to circulate, assess, and make real-time decisions about which student responses to use and why, making it far more adaptive than a simple 'now you try' instruction.

A 'You do, then I do' inversion can be strategically superior when the purpose is activating and exposing prior knowledge before instruction -- the teacher then uses student work as the entry point for explanation, not as the endpoint.

Questioning during the 'I do' phase is not optional: sustained teacher exposition is an attention threat, and embedding comprehension-check questions throughout the modelling phase keeps students cognitively active rather than passive observers.

The model is not rigid -- when students already have the relevant schema, skipping the 'We do' and moving directly from teacher model to independent practice avoids the patronising effect of scaffolding students who don't need it.
quotes: 'I do, We do, You do' refers to the back and forth exchange between teacher and students in any given learning exchange. It typically involves the teacher modelling and explaining directly during the 'I do' phase.
If the transfer is too fast (for example, 'I do' straight to 'You do') then understanding is likely to be less secure than if the gradual exchange of the 'We do' phase is included.
In this phase of the technique, students begin to take some responsibility for contributing to a shared solution or answer.
During the 'I do' phase, teachers usually ask lots of questions to check for student listening as this period of sustained teacher exposition can pose a threat to student focus.

When teachers are introducing a new concept, task or skill, they might use 'I do, We do, You do' exactly as explained above. This is because they need to initially explain the unknown to students and then gradually transfer the expectation of working independently with their new knowledge to students.
